extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (K-12 and higher-education institutions), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, campus legal counsel, and policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and requirements for how educational recipients must respond to sexual harassment under Title IX, including grievance-process rules, supportive measures, hearings, interplay with Title VII, and preemption of state law. Focused on institutional policies and procedures to ensure compliance with §§106.30, 106.44, and 106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures offered regardless of formal complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A complainant need not file a formal complaint for the recipient to provide supportive measures; §106.44(a) requires a recipient to offer supportive measures to a complainant irrespective of whether the complainant files a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures to any complainant who reports sexual harassment to help ensure complainants receive assistance. Supportive measures can be provided even if no formal grievance is filed and may help satisfy obligations under other legal frameworks (e.g., Faragher-Ellerth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt response and deliberate indifference standard
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient has actual knowledge of sexual harassment in its education program or activity, it must respond promptly in a manner that is not deliberately indifferent (§106.44(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are required to take timely action; promptness is required even if the exact timeframe for concluding the grievance may include reasonable delays for good cause (such as concurrent law enforcement activity). A recipient's response should not be so deficient as to constitute deliberate indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable treatment of complainants and respondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations do not favor either complainants or respondents and require the recipient's response to treat complainants and respondents equitably under §106.44(a) and §106.45(b)(1)(i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must offer supportive measures (or remedies where a determination of responsibility has been made) to complainants and must not impose disciplinary sanctions or other actions that are not supportive measures against a respondent unless the recipient first applies a grievance process that complies with §106.45.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance process prerequisite for disciplinary sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary sanctions or actions that are not supportive measures cannot be imposed against a respondent unless the recipient first applies a grievance process that complies with §106.45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects due process by requiring institutions to follow the §106.45 grievance process before imposing non-supportive disciplinary measures. Recipients must ensure their grievance procedures meet the regulatory requirements before sanctioning respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearing with cross-examination of relevant questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A live hearing is permitted in which a party's advisor may ask any questions that are relevant and that the rape-shield provision does not preclude; allowing all relevant questions provides a robust process for decision-makers to make informed determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department views live hearings with cross-examination as contributing to accurate and reliable outcomes. Decision-makers must be trained to serve impartially and avoid prejudgment, conflicts of interest, and bias. The rape-shield provision limits questioning only as to the complainant's sexual behavior or predisposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield limitation applies to complainant's sexual behavior/predisposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The rape shield provision in §106.45(b)(6) precludes questioning about the complainant's sexual behavior or disposition but does not preclude asking relevant questions about a respondent's sexual behavior or predisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, this means cross-examination may probe a respondent's sexual behavior or predisposition where relevant, while protections limit similar lines of inquiry directed at complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker impartiality and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers must receive training on how to serve impartially, including by avoiding prejudgment of the facts at issue, conflicts of interest, and bias pursuant to §106.45(b)(1)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is required to ensure hearings and determinations are fair and avoid preconceived conclusions. The preamble emphasizes this training as part of ensuring a fulsome process that does not deter complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retaliation protections for participants
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong retaliation provision in §106.71 protects any individual involved in a Title IX matter, including employees, from intimidation, threats, coercion, or other discrimination for participating or refusing to participate in any manner in an investigation, proceeding, or hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must prohibit and guard against retaliation toward complainants, respondents, witnesses, or others involved in the Title IX process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights to an advisor of choice for parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receipt of a formal complaint, recipients must provide written notice that parties may have an advisor of their choice, who may be but is not required to be, an attorney (§106.45(b)(2)(i)(B)), and parties must be afforded the same opportunities to have an advisor present during any grievance proceeding (§106.45(b)(5)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients cannot limit who may serve as an advisor; the regulation accommodates various advisor choices (attorneys, union representatives, parents acting as advisors where legally authorized). Institutions must provide parity of opportunity for both parties to have advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parent/guardian exercise of rights for minors or parties with guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party is a minor or has a guardian appointed, a parent or guardian with legal authority must be allowed to act on behalf of the party—file formal complaints, request supportive measures, review evidence, attend interviews/meetings/hearings, and exercise other rights under the regulations (§106.6(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a parent/guardian has the legal right to act is determined by state law, court orders, custody arrangements, or other sources. FERPA may affect the parent's ability to inspect education records; where FERPA would not permit access, the Title IX regulations provide the opportunity to inspect evidence directly related to the allegations in a formal complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of actual knowledge in elementary/secondary context
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's definition of actual knowledge in §106.30 includes all employees working in the recipient's education program or activity in the elementary and secondary context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because all employees are included in the definition of actual knowledge for K–12, recipients in elementary and secondary contexts have broader channels triggering the duty to respond promptly and not be deliberately indifferent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different legal standards under Title IX vs Title VII
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX and Title VII have different definitions and standards for sexual harassment: Title VII defines sexual harassment as severe or pervasive and includes negligence standards and vicarious liability, while Title IX applies a severe and pervasive standard and requires actual knowledge and a not-deliberately-indifferent response. Employers must be aware that complying with one does not automatically satisfy the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should craft policies that account for both frameworks where both statutes may apply; additional policies beyond Title IX may be needed to meet Title VII obligations. The Department clarifies nothing in these regulations derogates Title VII rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interplay with Faragher–Ellerth affirmative defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Title IX imposes a not-deliberately-indifferent standard, employers may still invoke the Faragher–Ellerth affirmative defense under Title VII (requiring reasonable care to prevent/correct harassment and that the employee unreasonably failed to use preventive/corrective opportunities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing supportive measures and offering the opportunity to file a formal complaint under §106.45, plus notice requirements (§106.8), may help employers argue they satisfied preventive or corrective obligations for the Faragher–Ellerth defense under Title VII. Recipients do not have to choose between asserting that defense under Title VII and complying with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and information requirements to employees (§106.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required under §106.8 to notify all employees and applicants for employment of the Title IX Coordinator's contact information and the grievance procedures and grievance process, including how to report or file a complaint of sex discrimination and how the recipient will respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear notice supports both Title IX responsiveness and an employer's potential argument that it provided preventive/corrective opportunities under other laws. Maintain accessible, up-to-date notices to employees and applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption of conflicting State or local law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department added §106.6(h) providing that to the extent of a conflict between State or local law and Title IX as implemented by §§106.30, 106.44, and 106.45, the obligation to comply with those sections is not obviated or alleviated by any State or local law; federal regulations have preemptive effect in actual conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may continue to comply with state/local laws that do not conflict. Some state laws may provide additional protections beyond these regulations; where no conflict exists, recipients should comply with both. The Department will not adopt state laws wholesale but will allow institutions to take additional actions where consistent with Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address conduct outside Title IX via other codes
rubrics_metrics.description: A dismissal of a formal complaint for Title IX purposes (e.g., because conduct did not occur in the recipient's program or activity) does not preclude a recipient from taking action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions retain the ability to address misconduct through non-Title IX processes when Title IX jurisdictional limits apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prompt timeframes and permitted delays for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(v) requires recipients to conclude the grievance process within reasonably prompt timeframes they have designated; good-cause temporary delays (including concurrent law enforcement activity) are permitted, provided the recipient still responds promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary delays (e.g., a ten-day delay during law enforcement action) can be consistent with the regulations if the recipient otherwise responds promptly and adheres to its designated reasonably prompt timeframes. Recipients should document reasons for delays and ensure overall promptness of response.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement to adopt a particular definition of consent
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 expressly states the Assistant Secretary will not require recipients to adopt a particular definition of consent with respect to sexual assault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may adopt definitions (including affirmative consent) as desired or as required by state law, but the Department will not mandate a specific consent definition under these regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERPA intersection with evidence inspection and review
rubrics_metrics.description: FERPA and its implementing regulations govern circumstances under which a parent or guardian may inspect and review a student's education records (34 CFR 99.10 and 99.12); where FERPA would not permit inspection, these Title IX regulations nonetheless provide a parent/guardian with the same opportunity to inspect and review evidence directly related to allegations in a formal complaint (§106.45(b)(5)(vi)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must balance FERPA obligations with the Title IX requirement to provide parties (and authorized parents/guardians) the opportunity to inspect and review evidence related to the formal complaint; apply FERPA rules and, where FERPA would not permit access, comply with the Title IX evidence-review requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: No derogation of employees' Title VII rights (§106.6(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.6(f) provides that nothing in this part shall be read in derogation of an individual's rights, including an employee's rights, under Title VII or its implementing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must understand that Title IX obligations do not eliminate or override employees' separate rights under Title VII, and compliance strategies should account for both regimes where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodating union representation and advisors during investigatory interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no inherent conflict between the final regulations and any requirement that a union representative be present for an investigatory interview that might lead to discipline; parties are afforded the same opportunities to have an advisor present during grievance proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should allow union representatives or other chosen advisors to attend investigatory interviews and grievance proceedings consistent with collective bargaining and state labor laws, while ensuring parity for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will not second-guess recipient factual determinations absent deliberate indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(b)(2) provides that the Assistant Secretary will not ordinarily second-guess a recipient's factual determinations regarding responsibility and will not deem a recipient deliberately indifferent solely because the Assistant Secretary would have reached a different outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives recipients discretion in factfinding; however, deference is limited—actions still must not amount to deliberate indifference. If a matter is referred to the EEOC under Title VII, the EEOC will make independent determinations under its regulations.
